Fitting methods for estimating scales of effect

Source: R/doc_fitting_methods.R
multiScaleR-fitting-methods.Rd

multiScale_optim() estimates scales of effect through one of several backends, chosen with its backend argument. A backend is the computational route that searches over kernel scales and fits the model at each candidate. Backends differ in the models they accept, the parameters they estimate together, and the uncertainty they can report. This page states the requirements and reporting rules of each backend. To choose a backend for your model, start with vignette("v07-fitting-methods", package = "multiScaleR"), which compares them on one data set.

Compare the backends

backendModels it fitsEstimated in one searchUncertainty for the scales
"refit" (default)Any model that stats::update(), the unmarked equivalent, or a refit_fn can refitKernel scales and shapes. The model's own parameters are refit at every candidateHessian (Wald) standard errors for smooth kernels. Profile likelihood with summary(fit, profile = TRUE)
"profile_glm"Gaussian identity, Poisson log, and binomial logit glm() fits, and NB2 log-link fitsKernel scales and NB2 theta. Coefficients are solved at every candidateJoint Wald limits when the checks below pass
"joint_nb2"NB2 log-link fits, including the exact Poisson boundaryKernel scales, coefficients, and dispersionJoint Wald limits when the checks pass. None at the Poisson boundary
"joint_mixed"Poisson and NB2 glmmTMB fits with one random interceptKernel scales and all model parameters, with the random intercept integrated outWald limits for each scale that passes its checks. Profile likelihood with summary(fit, profile = TRUE). Coefficient uncertainty is conditional on the scales
"conditional_logit"Step-selection models from survival::clogit() or amt::fit_clogit()Smooth kernel scales and conditional-logistic coefficientsNone. Coefficient uncertainty is conditional on the scales

A conditional standard error treats the estimated scales as known. A joint standard error lets the scales and the coefficients vary together, so it also carries uncertainty about the scales. multiScale_bayes() is a separate route that samples or approximates a posterior instead. See multiScaleR_bayes and the Bayesian vignettes.

The default refit backend

How the search works

The default backend uses the L-BFGS-B algorithm (a bounded quasi-Newton search) to maximize the log-likelihood over sigma, and over shape for the "expow" kernel. At each candidate scale it refits the model, so the regression coefficients take their fitted values for that scale. Candidate scales that leave a covariate undefined at a modeled observation are rejected, so every candidate is compared on the same sample. The final sample_size entry of diagnostics() reports the prepared and fitted row counts. For unmarked data with repeated sites, it also reports the number of distinct prepared spatial sites.

Standard errors and intervals

Standard errors are Hessian-based approximations from this outer search. A nonfinite, singular, or non-positive-definite Hessian gives missing standard errors and a retained diagnostic, and the raw Hessian is kept. So does a Hessian built partly from a failed refit: a refit that fails returns a large penalty, and a finite-difference point that lands on one gives an absurdly large curvature. This case also gives a warning, because it means the model is hard to refit near the estimate.

A smooth kernel or shape parameter within 1e-5 of a search bound, on the log scale, invalidates the Wald approximation for that parameter. Its standard error and Wald limits are withheld. The other smooth parameters keep Wald standard errors from their own block of the Hessian, which holds the bounded parameters fixed at their bounds; diagnostics(fit)$refit_hessian$conditional_on names those bounded parameters. The raw Hessian, the original curvature status, and a table of parameter bounds stay in diagnostics(fit)$refit_hessian. A lower bound of zero is flagged only when it is reached. This flag is numerical. It does not establish that a scale is identified or give a calibrated interval. Native coefficient covariance still conditions on the selected kernels, and likelihoods and parameter counts are unchanged.

Hard-radius covariates (landscape metrics, unweighted surface metrics, and every scale under kernel = "fixed") have a likelihood that changes in steps as the radius grows. They receive no Hessian standard error or Wald limit. Their raw Hessian rows remain for compatibility and diagnostics but are not inverted. See multiScaleR-kernels.

Summary methods report profile-likelihood intervals for sigma once profile_sigma() has been run on the fit, and Hessian-based intervals otherwise. summary(fit, profile = TRUE) computes profile-likelihood intervals directly.

Profile hard radii over a grid

The radius_grid argument is experimental, so its behavior may change in a later release without a deprecation period. Supply it to the refit backend for a likelihood profile over hard radii. At each combination of radii, the model refits its coefficients and any native nuisance parameters on the same observations. When Gaussian, exponential, or exponential-power kernels supply smooth predictors, a bounded search starts afresh at each combination and refits every smooth bandwidth and applicable shape. Use par to give the first smooth start in the usual parameter layout.

The largest eligible native log-likelihood selects the combination. Exact ties favor the smallest radii, in model predictor order. Inspect failed combinations and likelihood plateaus in diagnostics(fit)$radius_profile. Hard radii have no standard error or confidence interval. Smooth standard errors and Wald limits, when available, condition on the selected radii.

The grid refits serially. It accepts ordinary lm(), glm(), and MASS::glm.nb() fits, and complete one-case conditional-logistic models, each with a retained model frame. Fixed predictors, including fixed-radius metrics, can accompany the optimized predictors. Retain raw cells and matching model row IDs, and omit join_by, custom refit functions, and start screening. For step selection, supply one case and at least one available alternative per stratum, with an unweighted, unpenalized native likelihood.

Analytic GLM backends

"profile_glm" and "joint_nb2" evaluate the likelihood and its derivatives directly rather than refitting the model through update(). This makes joint uncertainty possible.

Models and data they accept

Both need a smooth kernel (Gaussian, exponential, or exponential power) and a glm or MASS::glm.nb object that retains its model frame. Fit a Gaussian model with glm(family = gaussian()), because an lm() fit is rejected. "profile_glm" supports the Gaussian identity, Poisson log, binomial logit, and NB2 log links. NB2 has variance \(\mu + \mu^2/\theta\), and theta is estimated alongside the kernel parameters even when the starting GLM used a fixed theta. "joint_nb2" requires an NB2 log-link model.

The retained model-frame rows define the fitting sample. Their row names must match unique prepared point IDs, so preserve them through any subsetting. Kernel means and standard deviations use only these rows, and no observations are dropped during the search.

A binomial response may be:

  • numeric 0/1 or logical FALSE/TRUE (Bernoulli observations);

  • a two-level factor, with success in its second level;

  • cbind(successes, failures) with positive trial totals. Logical count columns stand for zero and one counts without changing the trial totals.

Response-scale predictions are success probabilities. Positive whole-number frequency weights are allowed for count and binomial models. Gaussian weights must all equal one. Proportion responses and precision weights are not supported.

Formula terms

Numeric kernel predictors may enter native R product, crossing, and nesting terms, including factor interactions and products of optimized predictors. The native terms and fitted contrast coding define the coefficient layout, and every kernel, coefficient, and cross derivative enters the joint uncertainty.

Scalar arithmetic on kernel values inside I(), and the base functions exp, log, sqrt, sin, cos, and tan, keep their native coefficient basis and analytic derivatives. Their inputs must be optimized kernel values or literal constants, and a nonfinite result is an error.

Cubic splines::ns() and splines::bs() terms also work when you write out literal fixed knots and two increasing Boundary.knots. All basis columns share the ecological scale of their source, including in factor interactions. Knots are in the units of the modeled predictor. The analytic GLM, conditional-logistic, and joint mixed searches keep their candidate-specific standardization and its derivatives, so fixed standardized knots are not fixed thresholds of raw cover. Bayesian targets keep their frozen reference transformation instead: with a fixed reference, convert raw knots and boundaries with its center and SD before writing them into the formula. Basis values and their derivatives update at each candidate scale, while the knots, the coefficient basis, and any priors stay fixed. Only cubic bases with distinct, strictly interior knots are supported. Adaptive df recipes, repeated or boundary knots, and other degrees need the refit backend. Natural-spline tails are linear on the link scale. These are unpenalized bases of fixed complexity, with no smoothing-variance uncertainty and no monotonicity constraint.

GAMs keep their smooth terms and penalties only through the refit backend. They are not treated as ordinary unpenalized GLMs here.

Not supported: fixed inputs inside a dynamic expression, adaptive dynamic bases, nondifferentiable or arbitrary functions, kernel-dependent offsets, hard-radius metrics, random effects, and zero inflation. Put offsets in the formula with offset() rather than in the separate offset argument.

How the search works

Both backends run full multi-start searches in serial by default. Use n_cores = 1, start_strategy = "single", and profile_control. They do not accept refit_fn or join_by. Every winning start must pass both the optimizer's convergence check and a projected-gradient check.

For "profile_glm", regression coefficients are solved by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) at each candidate. A full-rank NB2 fit whose iterations fail receives a coefficient refinement that uses the analytic score and observed information. The Gaussian residual standard deviation is profiled at its maximum likelihood estimate. Independent native likelihoods have verified the fitted objective in simulations of the supported families. This backend is experimental, and the calibration of its scale intervals is not established. Simulations found Wald undercoverage even among fits that passed the curvature checks. For single-kernel NB2 models, scale_inference() examines the full likelihood range and can assess individual scale values with a parametric bootstrap.

"joint_nb2" uses L-BFGS-B to estimate the kernel parameters, the coefficients, and \(\rho = \log(1 + \alpha)\) together, where \(\alpha = 1/\theta\). At rho = 0 the likelihood is exactly Poisson. Each candidate must also agree, within 1e-5 negative log-likelihood units, with an independently optimized conditional coefficient fit. Start records keep failures, projected gradients, conditional likelihood gaps, and warnings. dispersion_est adds alpha and exact_poisson, and a boundary estimate has theta = Inf. The model is still NB2, so its parameter count includes dispersion at the boundary. Its conditional coefficient summary uses the Poisson GLM summary at that boundary; see dispersion_est for the NB2 boundary details. The profile_fit parameter vector holds the log kernel parameters followed by rho, and joint_par adds the regression coefficients. Interior joint covariance from vcov() uses log(theta) coordinates, as for "profile_glm".

For NB2 models in either backend, profile_control$coefficient_start = "warm" reuses conditional regression coefficients within each search. The default is "cold". Warm continuation resets at every independent start and falls back to cold initialization if its score or rank checks fail. Final likelihood checks always use independently initialized coefficients. Counts and fallback reasons are stored in profile_fit$coefficient_audit.

Run joint_nb2 starts in parallel

For "joint_nb2" only, profile_control$worker_pool spreads the independent starts over a PSOCK cluster you create with parallel::makePSOCKcluster(). It does not reduce the number of starts or change any uncertainty rule. Keep n_cores = 1, because the pool size sets the number of workers. Workers must load the same installed package code as the main session. Each start keeps its cold terminal audit, and results keep their original start order. Worker coefficient audits are stored in profile_fit$worker_coefficient_audits, and coefficient_audit then covers the final evaluation in the main session. Later profile and bootstrap inference stays serial.

You own the pool. Create it once, pass profile_control = list(worker_pool = pool) to each call, and close it with parallel::stopCluster() when finished, including after errors (use on.exit() inside your own function). Pool connections are not stored in the fitted object. Separate processes duplicate the data and package memory, so check estimate_multiscale_ram() first. Pool startup also checks the binned data against 75 percent of physical RAM, allowing four copies of the data and 1 GiB per process for the main session and the workers. This is a planning estimate, not a guarantee of peak memory. Startup can outweigh the gain for short jobs. Set math-library thread limits before creating workers to avoid nested parallel computation.

Uncertainty rules

Joint observed information includes kernel, coefficient, and dispersion cross derivatives. Default scale limits are normal approximations on the log scale. Wald uncertainty is withheld when any of these holds:

  • a parameter sits at a search bound;

  • the information is not positive, or its scaled condition number is at least 1e8;

  • a log-kernel standard error exceeds one;

  • competing starts lie more than 0.5 log units apart within a 95 percent likelihood threshold;

  • a Poisson fit at the selected scales comes within that same likelihood threshold of the NB2 fit;

  • the fit sits on the exact Poisson boundary.

These are screening rules, not a proof that the scales are identified. The Poisson comparison is conservative and is not a formal model test; reoptimizing the Poisson scales could reveal more compatibility. A separate near-Poisson diagnostic flags max(mu/theta) < 0.01. A finite upper theta bound does not establish a finite dispersion maximum. The marginal covariance and Hessian are missing whenever joint uncertainty is unavailable.

A kernel parameter at a search bound does not withhold joint uncertainty when every other rule passes for the remaining parameters. Joint covariance and joint prediction uncertainty then hold the bounded kernel parameters fixed at their bounds. They come from the observed information with those parameters removed, which must be positive and well conditioned, with every remaining log-kernel standard error at most one. Competing modes, a dispersion bound, a Poisson-compatible NB2 fit, or every kernel parameter at a bound still withholds them. vcov(fit) returns zero rows and columns for the held parameters, the marginal Hessian is missing for them, and diagnostics(fit)$profile_glm$joint_conditional_on names them. uncertainty_available stays FALSE. The rule is the same for "profile_glm" and "joint_nb2".

The scale table applies the kernel-specific rules one parameter at a time. A kernel parameter loses its standard error and Wald limits only when it sits at a search bound, its own log-scale standard error exceeds one, or competing starts move it by more than 0.5 log units. Bounded kernel parameters are dropped from the observed information, so the remaining standard errors hold them fixed at their bounds, and diagnostics(fit)$profile_glm names them in scale_se_conditional_on. Unusable information, a dispersion bound, a Poisson-compatible NB2 fit, or the exact Poisson boundary still withholds every scale standard error.

Predictions with uncertainty = "conditional" at the Poisson boundary condition on both the kernel parameters and the boundary dispersion. They say nothing about uncertainty in either. See multiScaleR-prediction.

The conditional opt_mod keeps the standard GLM methods, but update(opt_mod) is disabled because its original call refers to the kernel values from before the search. Refit through multiScale_optim().

summary(fit, profile = TRUE) reoptimizes the other kernel parameters and the NB2 dispersion while it profiles each sigma. It reports the connected likelihood region around the selected solution. Limits that reach a search bound are labeled "profile-bound-limited" and are not fully resolved confidence limits. profile_sigma() instead holds the other kernel parameters fixed while it reestimates the coefficients and NB2 dispersion. Neither is guaranteed to find likelihood modes the search never visited.

Compare with an ordinary GLM

At the same fixed scales, with the same rows, design, offset, and response coding, the analytic binomial likelihood is the ordinary binomial GLM likelihood. You can check the retained conditional GLM against a separate glm() fit on the selected predictors. Do not compare the joint intervals with conditional GLM intervals, because the joint intervals also carry scale uncertainty. For a covariance comparison, use the same response form and weights. A vector response and a two-column response can give slightly different working covariance even when the coefficients and likelihood agree. aic_tab() and bic_tab() treat logical and numeric binomial responses as the same zero and one observations when the retained rows, trial totals, and likelihood weights agree.

Joint mixed backend

backend = "joint_mixed" needs the optional packages RTMB, TMB, and glmmTMB. It estimates the kernel scales and the model parameters together, integrating the random intercept out with the Laplace approximation. It fits log-link Poisson and NB2 glmmTMB models with one conditional random intercept, constant dispersion, and optional fixed-effects zero inflation. Use Gaussian or exponential kernels, retained model row names that match the prepared point IDs, and n_cores = 1. Numeric spatial predictors may enter native R crossing, nesting, and factor interaction terms.

Not supported: random slopes, more than one grouping term, spatial terms in the zero-inflation or dispersion formulas, non-unit weights, priors, parameter maps, and REML. Raw formula variables must be recoverable from the fitted model, so put offsets in the formula with offset().

Each start uses a fresh native fit, a joint Hessian check, and an independent native refit at its end point whose likelihood must agree within 1e-5. Failed starts stay in mixed_fit$start_results. If every start fails, the error condition carries start_results. No Hessian check is bypassed.

The result's opt_mod is the final native glmmTMB fit, and mixed_fit records the log scales, bounds, starts, every outcome, and the selected start. Narrow raw prediction data keep fixed-transform inputs for effect curves once the temporary refit data are gone. diagnostics(fit)$joint_mixed reports eligibility and scale-boundary flags. As with the analytic GLM backends, an estimate whose distance approaches max_D records the max_distance diagnostic and warning code, and fit$next_run suggests a follow-up max_D and starts.

Scale standard errors come from the joint Hessian of the selected start, which TMB computes for the Laplace-approximated likelihood with every model parameter free. fit$scale_est$SE is sigma times the standard error of log(sigma), and summary(fit) reports Wald limits on the log scale, as for "profile_glm". The checks match that backend, one scale at a time. A scale within 1e-5 of a search bound on the log scale loses its standard error, and the other scales hold it fixed at its bound. A scale also loses its standard error when its log-scale standard error exceeds one, or when another start within the 95 percent likelihood threshold moves it by more than 0.5 log units. A Hessian that is not positive definite, or unusable covariance, withholds every scale standard error. diagnostics(fit)$joint_mixed gives the status, the reason for each scale, and the bounded scales held fixed. Legacy scale Hessians stay NA.

Treat these limits with caution. In a simulation with one Gaussian kernel mean and 200 points in 40 sites, 95 percent Wald intervals held the true sigma in 77 percent to 97 percent of interior fits, depending on the scale and response family. They fell short where the likelihood was sharply peaked near the estimate but stayed close to its maximum over a wider range of scales. The limits describe local curvature only, and coefficient and prediction covariance still condition on the selected scales. Use predict(fit, se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional") or predict(fit$opt_mod, ...). This backend does not extend the single-predictor NB2 contract of scale_inference().

summary(fit, profile = TRUE) reports profile-likelihood limits instead. For each scale in turn, it holds sigma at candidate values and refits the native glmmTMB model, the same new fit that checks each start. The coefficients, the random-intercept standard deviation, and any NB2 dispersion are re-estimated, and the random intercept is integrated out as in the fit. With several scales, the other scales are re-estimated too, on the joint likelihood from the optimum of each eligible start, and a native refit checks that value. As for the analytic GLM backends, the limits bound the connected region around the estimate where the likelihood-ratio statistic stays below the 95 percent chi-square quantile with one degree of freedom. A limit that reaches a search bound is labeled "profile-bound-limited" and is not a fully resolved confidence limit. Every scale gets profile limits, including one whose standard error is withheld, for example at a search bound. Profiling stops with an error when a refit fails or finds a better optimum than the fit, and it needs the optional packages and the refit data stored in mixed_fit. In the same simulation, profile intervals held the true sigma in 842 of 900 data sets (89 percent to 96 percent by scale and family), against 821 of 899 for the Wald intervals. Where Wald coverage was lowest, NB2 at a true sigma of 240, the profile intervals held it in 133 of 150 data sets and the Wald intervals in 115 of 149. Profile limits therefore describe scale uncertainty better than the Wald limits, but they can still fall short of nominal coverage, as they did in that scenario. Each profile took a median of 2 to 5 seconds there. profile_sigma() instead holds the other scales at their estimates.

Conditional-logistic backend

backend = "conditional_logit" fits step-selection models with the exact likelihood of a finite choice set: one used step and at least one available step per set. See vignette("v10-step-selection", package = "multiScaleR").

Models and data it accepts

Use a survival::clogit() model fitted with model = TRUE, a survival::coxph() model with a constant-time response such as Surv(rep(1, nrow(dat)), case), or an amt::fit_clogit() wrapper, with Gaussian or exponential kernels and one bare strata(choice_id) term. A quoted choice-set ID is still one bare variable, and special-call text inside a quoted predictor name is not read as a Cox special term. IDs must identify sets uniquely across animals and bursts, and row names must match the prepared point IDs. Prepare complete sets before fitting. Omitted missing rows, subsets, weights, robust clustering, and special Cox terms are rejected. Keep the available steps fixed throughout the search.

Numeric kernel predictors may enter native R interaction, crossing, and nesting terms, including crosses with factors or other optimized predictors. Fixed transformations and offsets keep their native meaning and saved training values. Kernel-only scalar arithmetic and the supported smooth base functions follow the same rules as the analytic GLM backends.

Optimized kernel-weighted surface SQ predictors are supported when the matching raw buffers are retained. They use the weighted root-mean-square deviation, not the sample SD within a hard radius. Their scales are estimated separately, and prediction needs the same source and metric specifications and the training normalization. Fixed-radius metrics can enter as fixed predictors. Their original prepared numeric columns must be retained in the native model frame, and new predictions need those columns unless include_fixed = TRUE verifies and reuses their original normalization (see prepare_prediction()).

Not supported: hard-radius landscape and surface metrics with estimated radii, adaptive dynamic bases, arbitrary or nondifferentiable functions, fixed context inside a dynamic expression, and kernel-dependent offsets.

How the search works

The backend runs independent L-BFGS-B starts in serial, with cold coefficient initialization and a cold native survival refit at every end point. A start is eligible when it converges, has a small projected score, agrees in likelihood and coefficients, has well-conditioned coefficient information, and agrees with the native covariance. Failed attempts and warnings stay explicit in profile_fit$start_results. If every start fails, the error condition carries start_results. profile_fit$starts stores the log-scale starting values, and winner identifies the selected record. After the original joint point passes the native agreement checks, cold native coefficients may refine its terminal score if the objective does not increase and the score improves. Both scores and the refinement flag are kept, and the eligibility threshold is unchanged.

What the fit keeps

The final opt_mod is the native conditional fit, with amt metadata when supplied. If the original fitting call no longer exposes its raw data, retained model-frame values support fixed transformations, factors, and compound offsets without inverting them. Cold native refits keep the original prediction transformations, including learned polynomial bases. Prediction for new data still needs the raw inputs named in the formula. The internal prediction record omits duplicate fitting data to save space; the original model stays in fitted_mod_original. Updating the conditional fit needs explicit data with kernel covariates that are already standardized; otherwise rerun the original multiscale fit.

Scale standard errors and joint prediction uncertainty are withheld. Coefficient covariance conditions on the selected scales and does not correct for temporal dependence among steps.

Movement terms

The original amt proposal distributions are unchanged. Apply amt's movement-distribution updates to opt_mod when they suit the movement terms in your model. Movement terms must match the available-step proposal. The backend does not add them, check a sampling interval, or calibrate population inference.

Covariate types and transformations

The analytic backends support optimized kernel means and kernel-weighted surface SQ (the weighted root-mean-square deviation), alone or together. Weighted SQ uses retained raw cell buffers with Gaussian or exponential kernels. Estimating the radius of any other surface metric needs the refit backend. Kernel means need bin = TRUE in kernel_prep(). Models with only surface metrics need explicit preparation row IDs and raw buffers, without binned summaries. See msr_vars() for how each covariate type is defined.

A fixed-radius metric enters the native numeric design as an ordinary predictor, with no scale parameter, in every backend and in multiScale_bayes(). Its original prepared values and normalization must stay recoverable from the native model frame. If every covariate is fixed, there is no scale to estimate, so fit the model directly to the prepared columns.

Under the "expow" kernel, a hard-radius predictor has no shape parameter. Its reported shape and shape standard error are NA, and model selection leaves the unused shape position out of the parameter count. The starting parameter vector keeps its full layout, so give a finite positive placeholder for that position when you supply par.

By default (covariate_transform = "candidate"), each optimized covariate is centered and scaled again at every candidate scale, so a coefficient describes a change of one standard deviation. The refit backend also accepts covariate_transform = "raw", which keeps optimized kernel and metric values in their own units. The fit records centers of zero and scales of one and reuses them for prediction, effect curves, and spatial cross-validation; they are never re-estimated from a prediction batch. Fit the starting model in those raw units, including any fixed spline knots. Raw mode does not change upstream surface reference normalization or the transforms of fixed metrics, and Bayesian targets are unaffected.

The Bayesian route also accepts weighted SQ, with a fixed pooled reference normalization and proper priors. Neither the candidate standardization nor the raw transform of multiScale_optim() is substituted into a Bayesian target.

Distance-removal models

Native distance-removal (GDR) models from unmarked use the refit backend. make_gdr_refitter() provides an opt-in native C or TMB refit function when you need independent starts and retained audits. It freezes the evaluated settings and keeps the final native covariance. TMB needs explicit tmb_settings, starts in constructor order including log-SDs, and native joint covariance checks. Its intermediate fits still compute sdreport.

Identified native GDR response fields (fit_gdr_response_field()) need a serial scale search: n_cores = 1 and PSOCK = FALSE. A NULL core count selects one for this route. Sending native fits to parallel workers has not been qualified.

Only active GDR component formulas identify spatial predictors. Availability is inactive for a single primary period, and the distance formula is inactive for a uniform key. Optimized static site covariates must not share names with columns in the native yearly or observation covariate tables. Dot formulas use the original component's available training columns.

Native GDR models with active formula offsets or TMB zero inflation are rejected before fitting, model selection, or prediction. In the audited unmarked 1.5.2 provider, offsets did not enter the fitted likelihood and the TMB zero-inflated Poisson likelihood ignored its zero-inflation parameter. multiScaleR does not remove offsets, switch engines, change parameter counts, or substitute uncertainty estimates for these cases. Offset-free C zero-inflated Poisson models keep their native likelihood and parameter count. See vignette("v12-distance-removal", package = "multiScaleR").

Control settings

profile_control is a named list. Entries a backend does not accept are an error.

EntryBackendsDefaultWhat it controls
n_startsanalytic GLM, joint_mixed, conditional_logit6Number of deterministic kernel starts
startsanalytic GLM, joint_mixed, conditional_logitNULLMatrix of explicit starts, one row per start (see below)
iter.maxanalytic GLM, conditional_logit500Iteration limit for each L-BFGS-B search
eval.maxanalytic GLM1000Evaluation limit for later profile and inference refits, which use conditional fitting
gradient_toleranceanalytic GLM, conditional_logit0.001Largest projected gradient a winning start may have
kernel_engineanalytic GLM, conditional_logit"reference""stream" computes kernel values and derivatives with less copying
theta_boundsanalytic GLMc(1e-4, 1e5); c(1e-4, Inf) for joint_nb2Search bounds for NB2 theta
theta_startanalytic GLMNULLStarting NB2 theta
coefficient_startanalytic GLM, NB2 only"cold""warm" reuses coefficients within a search
worker_pooljoint_nb2 onlyNULLPSOCK cluster for running starts in parallel

Each row of starts holds positive kernel scales in internal distance units (map distance divided by unit_conv), followed by shapes for "expow", in model predictor order. Explicit starts replace the deterministic scale starts, and par, if supplied, is added first. All independent starts are kept. NB2 dispersion starts cycle through the initial theta, 0.3, 2, and 20 within the bounds. For "profile_glm", theta bounds must be positive, increasing, and at most 1e6. For "joint_nb2", the upper bound must stay infinite and the lower bound must be at least 1e-8. Each "joint_nb2" kernel start is tried at the exact Poisson boundary and at an interior dispersion, giving 12 fits with the default six kernel starts.

The "stream" kernel engine traverses the prepared matrices contiguously, copies them less, and caches response-only NB2 terms. It keeps the same starts, likelihood, and uncertainty checks. It uses extra temporary vectors proportional to the number of observations and can speed up larger binned inputs. For smooth weighted SQ predictors under "conditional_logit", it also computes values and scale derivatives in compiled code, reusing work buffers across sites, with temporary storage proportional to the largest retained site buffer.

See also

multiScale_optim() for the arguments, multiScaleR for the fitted object, multiScaleR-kernels for kernels and hard radii, multiScaleR-prediction for prediction uncertainty, and vignette("v07-fitting-methods", package = "multiScaleR") and vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR").
